title: Breaking news of a sudden death after trauma

header.contentArea: Breaking bad news; death and the coroner

related.why: Breaking bad news when there is time to plan
The trauma resuscitation that came before this conversation

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the trauma team
brief.scenario: James O'Brien, 35, was the driver in a high-speed collision on the motorway. He was unresponsive when paramedics reached him and had a cardiac arrest on arrival. Despite 40 minutes of resuscitation, he died at 14:10. His wife, Sarah, has just arrived. Police are at the hospital. Your consultant has asked you to speak to her with the nurse in charge.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: She needs to know he has died, in plain words, early. Then stay with her.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: 'We lost him' or 'he passed away': she may not understand.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Check the facts and his identity, hand over your bleep, and take the nurse in with you.

grid.label: Preparation
grid.fail: Speaks to her standing in the corridor, bleep going, alone.
grid.pass: Checks the facts and his identity first; private room; sits down; nurse present; bleep handed over.
grid.high: Asks whether she has anyone with her or would like someone called before starting.

grid.label: What she knows and the warning shot
grid.fail: Opens with the death, or with a long description of the resuscitation.
grid.pass: Asks what she has been told, then gives a warning shot and pauses.
grid.high: A brief lead-in in her terms: serious crash, unresponsive at the scene, heart stopped, everything tried.

grid.label: Telling her clearly
grid.fail: Uses euphemisms ('we lost him', 'passed away') or stays vague.
grid.pass: 'I'm very sorry. James has died.' Says 'died' or 'dead'.
grid.high: Uses his name, then stays silent; repeats 'he has died' if she asks again or doesn't take it in.

grid.label: Emotion and her questions
grid.fail: Fills the silence, gives false reassurance, or overloads her with clinical detail.
grid.pass: Acknowledges her distress, lets her lead, answers honestly within what he knows.
grid.high: Answers 'Did he suffer?' honestly from the facts: unresponsive from when paramedics reached him; offers the consultant for more detail.

grid.label: The coroner
grid.fail: Says the hospital will issue the death certificate, or suggests the police think James did wrong.
grid.pass: A death after injury must be reported to the coroner, who may order a post-mortem; this is routine.
grid.high: The death can't be registered until the coroner allows; a coroner's officer will contact her; police investigate every serious collision.

grid.label: Viewing and support
grid.fail: Leaves her alone, or refuses to let her see him.
grid.pass: Offers to take her to see him; bereavement service, written information, chaplaincy; arranges someone to be with her.
grid.high: Explains touching him may need the coroner's agreement; offers a later meeting with the consultant.

grid.label: Closing the conversation
grid.fail: Leaves without a plan or contact.
grid.pass: Summarises next steps, gives a named contact, checks how she will get home.
grid.high: Records the conversation, tells the consultant, and informs his GP.

failures.move: Saying 'we lost him' or 'he passed away'.
failures.consequence: She may not understand he has died; she has to ask again or holds false hope.

failures.move: Saying 'he felt nothing at all' without knowing it.
failures.consequence: False reassurance that the post-mortem or inquest may contradict, damaging trust.

failures.move: Telling her the hospital will issue the death certificate today.
failures.consequence: The coroner must be told; she makes plans that then fall through.

failures.move: Starting the conversation standing in a corridor.
failures.consequence: No privacy or support at the worst moment of her life.

recovery.line: I'm sorry, I need to be clear: James has died.

recovery.when: She asks something you don't know
recovery.line: I don't know, and I don't want to guess. I'll find out or ask the consultant to talk to you.

knowledge.fact: A doctor must notify the coroner if the death may be due to trauma or injury.
The coroner may order a post-mortem; the death can't be registered until the cause is known, but an interim certificate of the fact of death can be given.
Relatives can normally see the body; touching may not always be possible, for example when evidence is needed.
Police may investigate a death separately from the coroner.
Organ donation directly from the ED is uncommon; tissue donation is possible up to 24–48 hours after death.

recall.think: She may not understand he has died if you soften it.
do: Facts checked, private room, nurse, bleep off

recall.finish: Clear news, honest answers, coroner explained, support arranged.

partner.opening: Mrs O'Brien has just been shown into the relatives' room. Please go in when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Sarah O'Brien, 34, James's wife. You got a call from the police to come to hospital after a crash; you don't know how bad it is. Opening line: "Where is he? Can I see him?" If the candidate uses a euphemism ('lost him', 'passed away'), ask: "So is he alive or not?" When told clearly he has died, fall silent, then cry. Then ask, in this order, if the candidate leaves space: "Did he suffer?", "Why are the police here? Did he do something wrong?", "Can I see him? Can I hold him?" If the candidate gives a detailed medical account, look lost. Hidden concern, revealed only if asked what's worrying her: your two children are with a neighbour, and you don't know what to tell them.

reveals.trigger: Asks if anyone is with her

reveals.finding: "The kids are with a neighbour. What do I tell them?"

push.question: Why does the coroner need to know?
push.expect: Death after trauma or injury must be reported; coroner may order a post-mortem; registration waits.

push.question: What support will you arrange?
push.expect: Viewing, bereavement service, written information, chaplaincy, someone with her, later meeting.

push.question: What will you do after the conversation?
push.expect: Record it, tell the consultant and GP, check she can get home safely.

curveballs.prompt: "He was on the donor register. Can he still help someone?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Thanks her; organ donation is unlikely after a death in the ED, but tissue donation may be possible; the specialist nurse will talk to her.
Use clear words like 'died', not 'gone to sleep'; offers written resources and bereavement support.
Doesn't speculate: the police investigation and the coroner will look at how it happened.

curveballs.prompt: "Someone must have made a mistake in here."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges her feelings, doesn't argue; offers a meeting with the consultant; the coroner's investigation looks at how he died.
